content: This document is an updated review of the role of lymphadenectomy in the surgical management of endometrial cancer. Lymphadenectomy involves the removal of pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes and has been widely used as part of the FIGO staging system for endometrial cancer. Approximately 10% of women who are initially thought to have cancer confined to the uterus are found to have lymph node metastases. While some studies have suggested that lymphadenectomy may improve survival, these studies were not randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and the therapeutic benefit of treating pelvic lymph nodes remains unclear. Instead, lymphadenectomy may primarily serve to stratify patients into prognostic groups. Previous Cochrane reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs have shown no survival advantage for routine adjuvant radiotherapy aimed at treating possible lymph node metastases in women with early-stage endometrial cancer. Furthermore, lymphadenectomy carries significant risks of both short-term and long-term complications, making it essential to evaluate its clinical value. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of lymphadenectomy in managing endometrial cancer. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of databases, clinical trial registries, scientific meeting abstracts, and reference lists of relevant studies. They also consulted experts in the field. The review included RCTs and quasi-RCTs comparing lymphadenectomy to no lymphadenectomy in adult women diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Hazard ratios (HRs) for overall survival and progression-free survival, as well as risk ratios (RRs) for adverse events, were pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The search identified 978 unique references, of which three RCTs met the inclusion criteria. However, one small RCT lacked sufficient data for inclusion in the meta-analysis. The two included RCTs involved 1945 women, with survival data based on 1851 participants. These studies had an overall low risk of bias, meeting four of the assessment criteria. The third study had an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient information on random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting. The meta-analysis showed no differences in overall survival or recurrence-free survival between women who underwent lymphadenectomy and those who did not. The pooled hazard ratio for overall survival was 1.07 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 1.43), and for recurrence-free survival, it was 1.23 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.58). These results were based on moderate-quality evidence from 1851 participants in two studies. There was no significant difference in the risk of direct surgical morbidity between the two groups. However, women who underwent lymphadenectomy had a significantly higher risk of surgery-related systemic morbidity (RR 3.72, 95% CI 1.04 to 13.27) and lymphoedema or lymphocyst formation (RR 8.39, 95% CI 4.06 to 17.33). These findings were based on high-quality evidence from 1922 participants in two studies. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to suggest that lymphadenectomy reduces the risk of death or disease recurrence in women with presumed stage I endometrial cancer. However, lymphadenectomy is associated with a higher likelihood of surgery-related systemic morbidity and lymphoedema or lymphocyst formation. Currently, there is no RCT evidence on the impact of lymphadenectomy in women with higher-stage disease or those at high risk of disease recurrence.
